\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated models (Qwen, Llama; DR\,$\leq$\,1\% under greedy constrained decoding), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%) as a consequence of per-relation independent enforcement; for poorly-calibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87\%\,$\to$\,1.27\%) by constraining type assignments to schema-valid values.
CF fallback ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR ($+$13.85\,pp). CF$\leftrightarrow$DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}).
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF violations.
CF type inconsistencies may propagate to downstream tasks that consume extracted triples (e.g., knowledge graph construction, question answering); the impact of such propagation has not been evaluated.
Entity F1 impact is model-dependent ($+$1.22\,pp for Qwen vs.\ $-$0.64\,pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%).
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations across all fine-tuned settings, both models and both datasets) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors correctly caught by constraints (28\%); Llama DocRED alone accounts for 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), reflecting weaker entity typing (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Schema coverage gaps (one-third of residual violations) arise because RE constraints are extracted from training-data type pairs, which may not cover all valid combinations; larger training sets or manual constraint table completion can reduce this gap.

\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
Zero-shot results cover three 7--8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4--8\% compared to $\sim$45\% for fine-tuned systems.
Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated only on 8B-class models.
Scaling to smaller models has not been verified, and the dual-factor pattern's predictive scope may differ at other scales.
Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%, R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; EE: RoV$\to$0\%, AC$\leq$0.8\%), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF (Qwen 1.18\%, Llama 0.46\% on SciERC) traces to schema-level type ambiguity (\textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X) rather than enforcement failure.
WikiEvents fine-tuning composability is preliminary (20-document test set, the full official split).
All main experiments use greedy decoding; our evaluation of beam search on the full SciERC test set (551 documents) and DocRED (50 zero-shot, 998 fine-tuned documents) across three models confirms compatibility (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}), but comprehensive evaluation across all decoding configurations remains future work.

\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
Scalability benchmarks up to 200 entity types and 1,000 relations show constant 2--3\% inference overhead and sub-second compilation ($<$0.5\,s; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}); however, the first-token uniqueness requirement for continuation masking may become a tokenizer-dependent bottleneck beyond this scale.
Our approach requires access to model logits for token-level masking, which excludes API-only models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude) where only output text is available; extending to API-only settings would require alternative enforcement mechanisms such as constrained sampling APIs or output reranking.
Continuation masking assumes each entity type name maps to a distinguishable token prefix sequence.
This assumption holds for our evaluation ontologies but may be challenged by ontologies with morphologically similar type names (e.g., \texttt{Protein} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Complex} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Domain}); when type names share a common prefix longer than one token, masking granularity depends on the tokenizer's subword segmentation.
Fine-tuning composability was validated exclusively with LoRA; full fine-tuning with an untuned learning rate underperforms LoRA (R-F1 37.89 vs.\ 43.77 on SciERC) but confirms that constraints remain effective (DR 2.74\%\,$\to$\,0\%; Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}); other fine-tuning methods may exhibit different constraint interaction patterns and warrant further investigation.

\paragraph{Layer contributions.}
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, DR=0.1484, R-F1=0.0823
Grammar-only eliminates RV and ET with no F1 impact while DR remains at 14.84\%, the ceiling of grammar-based decoding~\cite{geng2023gcd}; grammar-only CF is near-zero (0.08\%), so CF originates from the semantic layer.
Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% and cannot eliminate RV or ET; this is the \emph{enabling dependency}: adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

\paragraph{Comparison with constrained decoding baselines.}
\label{sec:constrained-baselines}
Our grammar-only ablation (row~2) implements the same constraint class as GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} and BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}---CFG-based vocabulary membership---eliminating RV and ET but reducing DR by only 24\%; OntoCoDec's Level~2 semantic layer yields 94\%, a 70\,pp gap beyond CFG expressiveness (Proposition~1).
Direct comparison with BoostCD is precluded by task (closed Wikidata IE, FlanT5-250M vs.\ open-schema 7--70B) and benchmark differences; our grammar-only row establishes functional equivalence at the shared Level~1 constraint class.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; type violation elimination ensures ontological consistency of constructed KGs independent of extraction F1, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), four models (7--70B), and three tokenizer families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral).
DR enforcement is precision-preserving (removed triples are 97.6--100\% hallucinated false positives), but introduces CF side-effects that are model- and schema-dependent (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuning resolves most CF ($\leq$1.2\%).
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR (DR $\leq$ 0.09\%) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally reduces CF, achieving zero violations on SciERC under favorable conditions (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation on 7--8B models with preliminary 70B results confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework, motivated by a decidability analysis establishing that IE type constraints require runtime state beyond CFG expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies (validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types). As a diagnostic tool, constraint tightness $\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes enforcement outcomes (94--99\% DR reduction at $\bar{\kappa}{<}0.5$ vs.\ 42--90\% at $\bar{\kappa}{>}0.8$; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
    \item A comprehensive evaluation of type constraint enforcement across 3 IE datasets, 4 models (7--70B), and 2 tasks: (a)~for RE, the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction while their composition yields 94--100\%, and that fine-tuning does not obviate constraints (residual DR 1--2\% at R-F1 40--46\%); (b)~preliminary event extraction results on WikiEvents demonstrate generalization to 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

We apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 roles, 27 entity types, 245 constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}) without modification.

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained EE produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV $>$85\%; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), with entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot process off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all models, which validates the tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE and SentencePiece.
Grammar-only eliminates EV but leaves RoV at 64--77\% and surfaces latent AC (8--14\%), consistent with DocRED's pattern (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); full S1 drives RoV to 0\%.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to semantically similar types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN).
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument structures increase entity reuse across slots.
Post-hoc filtering is impractical ($<$0.5\% arguments retained).
Unlike RE, EE shows measurable F1 gains: entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%, trigger F1 $+$1.5--1.8\,pp.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}

Per-document variance is high (Arg-F1 std/mean ${>}$\,0.5, with 35--47\% of documents scoring zero), confirming that the 20-document test set provides sufficient power to detect violation elimination but not to detect small F1 differences.
